pitch_detail.notes: P1 (5.11, about 50 m) starts by scrambling up and right to a pedestal with a single bolt; do not drift left toward the rap anchor, and belaying from the talus causes rope drag. P2 (5.11-, about 45 m) goes up and left to a rap anchor, then blocky ground to a tongue of clean rock, with loose blocks to watch for. P3 (5.12-, about 15 m) is a clean sculpted slab with a step-right crux, finishing on a sloping ledge under the overhanging Shield. Mostly less-than-vertical rock with some ledge scrambling.

P4 (5.12-, about 20 m) steps down right, then moves up jugs and trends left on airy edges to a stance in a dike; a straight-up direct variation is a closed project. P5 (5.13-, about 30 m) is the Dike pitch: the dike itself is about 5.11+, then a roughly V7 boulder crux on textureless pinches, then a 5.12 traverse right to a stance. P6 (5.11, about 30 m) is face climbing to a roof pull, then juggy sidepulls and edges to a corner belay.

P7 (5.12, about 30 m) follows a dihedral past a large rock scar, makes a hard step right on crimps, and rounds an arete to a sloping anchor stance before continuing through a roof to a second sloping stance; the line is widely rated one of the best pitches on the route. P8 (5.12, about 15 m) is a corner of laybacking and stemming to an airy lip, with the belay in an alcove. The key pinch through the roof is the crux of this section.

P9 (5.11-, about 30 m) climbs a left-facing corner using face holds, the crack and a juniper, then pulls right to a stance. P10 (5.11+, about 35 m) is a tricky slab to a good ledge that is a poor one-person bivy but suits a portaledge (extra bolts were added for that). P11 (5.12, about 36 m) is under-vertical climbing to a layback crux and the right edge of a small roof, then easier ground past a rap anchor to a ledge under the Big Overhang; loose rock on that ledge.

P12 (5.13-, about 45 m) goes straight up through choss below a small roof, boulders through a second roof, then trends left through slopers (about V6) to a shallow corner, passes a rap anchor, and finishes with a redpoint boulder (about V5) over a bulge; permadraws are in place and about five more draws are needed. P13 (5.12, about 20 m) is sidepulls and compression blocks to a boulder move at the lip. P14 (5.11-, about 20 m) is jugs and pockets past suspect rock, and P15 (5.12, about 35 m) is bulgy ground on unusual holds to a slightly overhanging crimp crux, then jugs left and up to a belay below cedars. Stick clips or rodeo-clipping the permadraws help on the hard sections of P14 and P15.

P16 (5.8, about 65 m) is hands on rock and feet on cedars to a rap anchor, then a corner to a stance under a slab. P17 (5.9, about 70 m) is easy slab to a rock with a rap anchor, over it to cracks and trees, right to regain rock, then heather and trees past a tree rap anchor to a two-bolt anchor just below the buttress summit; a few feet of simul-climbing may be needed. Minimally cleaned, with loose rock on the ledges.

review.changed: Kept the six stored section labels and wrote per-pitch detail (grades and approximate lengths as stated in the route description, put in notes because the page calls them approximations rather than measurements) inside each. No rappel_detail written: the sources give rappel OPTIONS (skip the P12/P13 belays via dedicated anchors, skip the near-P11-top anchor with an 80 m rope, rap the Dike pitch via its own anchor, rap P1 straight down to an intermediate rap and the talus) but no numbered station list or per-rappel lengths, so a station-by-station table would be invented. The stored rappels text already covers the single-70 m-rope point.
review.other_findings: Route page says 17 pitches while the AAJ article says 21 (stored beta already explains 17 linked vs 21 split). AAJ puts the 5.13 range at pitches 6 and 14 and the crux at 13 on its own numbering, which does not match the route page's numbering (crux 5.13- at P5 and P12); numbering differs by source, not reconciled.

pitch_detail.notes: Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Start on the steepening ground and follow cracks, belaying where comfortable or at the base of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Two options at the start: stay in the corner to the right the whole way, or take the middle cracks straight up to a tree. Either way, lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay after about 140 ft, below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that starts at #3 size and gets smaller, the trickiest section of the route; only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.

review.changed: Stored table was already close to the only full description; kept all labels and only sharpened P5 (two start options) and P7 (crack tapers from #3, hardest part). No rappel_detail: the sources only say the route is descended by rappel on a 60 m rope (some raps stretch it), with fixed anchors near P3, and that one rappel from the top reaches the gully; no station-by-station list was found. Mountaineers.org pages 403'd, so no second full source read.
review.other_findings: Route page header says 6 pitches (7th optional); stored pitches=7 is consistent. Stored rappels text says about nine rappels the whole way; that figure was not confirmed on the page I could read.

pitch_detail.notes: The first bolt blends into the rock and is hard to spot. Climb just above a left-trending overlap, then up past three bolts on thin, exciting face climbing to the anchor. Short runouts, and some poor rock between bolts.

Climb past two bolts to reach a crack. At the third bolt, traverse right and follow easier cracks to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can each be rappelled with a 70 m rope. Short runouts and some poor rock.

The long bolted pitch. A hard start for about the first 20 ft, then moderate 5.7–5.8 face and slab climbing to a tree anchor. The webbing at the tree may need replacing, so inspect it before trusting it.

Enjoyable cracks graded 5.6–5.7 lead to the top. Belay from a gear anchor or a tree. To descend, scramble back to the top of pitch 3 and rappel the route. A standard rack to 2 inches works, with extra runners for rope drag.

review.changed: Kept all four stored labels; added the webbing-check at the P3 tree and the rack note. No rappel_detail: the page says one 70 m rope is sufficient and to rappel from the top of P3, while the stored descent says a 70 m rope does not reach from the trees above P3's last bolt. Sources disagree and give no station list or per-rappel length, so no table. Only one full page was readable.
review.other_findings: Stored descent text (70 m does not reach from the P3 trees) contradicts the route page's 'one 70 m rope is sufficient'; one of them may come from a comment I could not load. Stored grade 5.10b vs page 5.10a/b, fine.

pitch_detail.notes: Dirty ledges lead to the first bolt, which is easiest to spot on the cleanest black-and-white granite. Follow the bolted slab up into a chute between two stands of trees and exit it to the right. Walk the belay uphill and left so the belayer sits under a right-facing corner.

Start in the brown right-facing corner with jagged rock and stem up to a roof. The moves at the roof are airy, but the crux is well bolted. Step right above the roof onto a short bolted slab that finishes at the anchor beneath a clean left-facing corner. Small optional gear is useful above the slab crux.

The only pitch that needs no trad gear. Begin on incut holds off the belay, follow the steep corner past the first roof (a brief move right, then back left onto the bolt line), and continue through the second overhang on white marbled rock. The top is a full-value arete: sustained face moves to the left, or bigger dynamic moves out right. A #1 or #2 cam is optional at the top. A first-time leader does well to clip the final hanger on the left and trend left. Stated length ranges from about 30 to 40 m.

Follow the right-trending corner ramp as it turns into an open book, with bolts visible ahead; skip the extra bolt far out right on the arete unless taking that variation. After three bolts, trend right along the arete to a bolted anchor on a slight ledge that looks straight across at the P5 crux. Variation 1: step right off the belay with small gear to huge exposed fins, then go straight up to a four-inch slung horn and rejoin the normal line. Variation 2: from the slung horn, traverse right about 20 m on clean rock to the large gully, staying in the corner on its right side, to a trad belay just right of the final bolted crux; protection is small gear plus .75, .3 and a 2 at the anchor, and it is a bit runout on easy ground.

Three bolts up a short, fun arete. Put a #1 cam in at the end of the overhang to protect the follower, then continue up and right to the bolted belay at the top of the wall. For the descent, look climber's left of this belay for a tree rappel anchor.

review.changed: Extended all five stored pitch notes from the route description (P2 anchor location and gear, P3 line through the roofs and the left-trending advice, both P4 variations, P5 protection and the tree anchor for the descent). Kept every stored label, bolt count, grade and length. Only one source page was readable; second-source searches found nothing else. No rappel table written: the only rappel beta is a tree anchor to the climber's left of the top belay and double 60 m ropes trending left to the next ledge; the number and location of later stations is not published.
review.other_findings: One search listing shows the route as 4 pitches while the description has a Pitch 5 heading; the 5-pitch table is consistent with the description. The stored descent text mentions a scree option that the source page does not state in the description I read.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at the top of the car-sized chockstone at the base of the east face. The first bolts are on slightly funky rock with yellow and orange lichen, but quality improves by the third bolt and the last five bolts are on superb granite. The climbing builds steadily on a steep, exposed face to a cryptic, steep crux (about V6) just below the anchor.

Almost no easy ground. The first half works up and around a vertical orange dike on interesting holds, leading into a short horizontal roof that needs blind reaches and heel hooks. Above the roof the angle eases only a little, with insecure moves to a small stance at the anchor.

A breather before the crux pitch. Step left off the belay and around the arete to a short, easy hand crack that leads to a larger arete. A few moves are funky and surprisingly hard, particularly for shorter climbers.

The money pitch. Scramble up the ramp to the left to a short flake, pass a few bolts of bouldery moves, then reach right to the start of the finger crack. Layback and jam the roughly 45-foot crack to a good jug flake and rest. From there small feet and crimps lead over the bulge in a V9/V10 boulder problem, finished with a mantel onto a short slab. Without beta or chalk it can feel much harder than its grade.

Ramble up the slab to the huge corner and roof overhead. Most of the pitch is jamming or laybacking on good holds. It steepens before a traverse out and right around the offwidth roof; undercling and layback the offwidth until it is possible to squeeze inside, where feet and hands are good and the climbing quickly eases. Gear in the protection list: a single #3 is needed only on this pitch.

A short stretch of 4th class leads to a bolt by a tree, where the belay is moved. Climb left up a ramp, mantel up and right onto the top of a large flake, and place a few small cams before setting off on insecure, funky jams. The difficulty tapers off and better locks appear higher.
Straight up small ledges through some loose rock, a bit runout but never hard. Gain the huge open corner and turn right onto fun, easy laybacking.

Jam and stem the left side of the overhanging open chimney until it is possible to stem out right. Avoid the large wedged block near the end of the pitch, and build the belay on the bolts out left so the rope does not pinch behind that block.

A few wide stems up the chimney reach the first bolt, then step left around the arete. Easy, enjoyable face climbing leads up and left toward the arete that divides the east and north faces, where the route meets Thin Red Line. Can be linked with pitch 10 if little gear is placed.

Easy but loose blocks just left of the arete lead to the top. From here the choice is about 150 m of 4th-class terrain to the true summit, or rappelling the route on a single 80 m rope; the anchors on the route were placed roughly 40 m apart.

review.changed: Kept every stored label, grade, length, bolt count and anchor. Extended the notes with the line description from the route page and the first-ascent write-up (pitch 1 and 2 character, how pitch 4 starts, pitch 5 gear, pitch 6 belay move, pitch 8 belay placement, pitch 9 link to Thin Red Line, anchor spacing). No rappel table: the only rappel beta is 'rappel the route on a single 80 m rope', anchors were drilled about 40 m apart, and no station-by-station description exists in any source I could read.
review.other_findings: A third-party write-up calls the route 11 pitches and 5.13d; the first-ascent article says 1,100 ft, IV 5.13+ with 'remaining six' pitches after the first four plus one, consistent with 10 pitches here. Stored P3 length/bolt counts could not be cross-checked. The first-ascent article mentions the team called P5 5.11 'hero climbing' but gives no further detail.

pitch_detail.notes: Low-angle, sometimes water-polished slab at 5.4-5.8, with runouts that can be long but on easy ground. The first two pitches link in one lead, and a competent party can run the next three and a half as a running belay to the top of the lower slabs. The pitch that reaches the first big ledge can be wet; a ramp on the left avoids it. P7 climbs a short 5.7 wall before easing back to slab. The whole route follows a gully slab, so anything knocked off above funnels straight down these pitches — the many bent hangers show it; do not linger below other parties.

A fun blocky ramp cutting through the steeper wall above the lower slabs, a full rope length from the base of that wall. Protection is sparse — two bolts of 5.7-5.8 at the start, a bolt about halfway and a fixed pin about 15 ft below the belay — but the climbing is easy. On the way down this ramp is downclimbed rather than rappelled.
The first 5.9 pitch, on steeper rock where the bolts are closer together as the moves get harder. It ends on a large ledge.
Easy climbing above the ledge. Bypass the chain anchors and scramble up to the base of the steep wall on the left, belaying on a flake below the bolt line of the next pitch.
The first 5.10 pitch: well-bolted, balancy face climbing that is a fair test for the upper crux. Stay on the bolt line; forcing moves off it makes the pitch harder.
A more moderate pitch (roughly 5.8) up to chains. The top of this pitch makes a worthwhile objective on its own; above it the rock and climbing are poorer.

Easy (about 5.0-5.8) but the most runout section, on fair, slightly polished rock that sheds stones onto parties below. P13 is a full rope length with small cams useful in flakes, and can be run as one lead to a second set of chains up and right. A moderate pitch with five or six bolts follows to a belay where the wall kicks back. P15's two bolts are easy to miss and P16-17 have only the stations. Where the wall kicks back, go left to a bolt, up and right to a belay between a stand of trees and a heather patch (about 40 m, two bolts), then right along an obvious ramp of roughly 120 ft to the headwall; the trees and heather are useful landmarks on the descent too. Parties most often get lost here.
The first pitch of the upper headwall, where the bolt line picks back up, finishing on a tricky friction slab (around 5.9).

The crux: a steep, sustained wall nearly a full 60 m rope length, needing around 17 draws (bring long ones or back-clean). Its anchor has no chains; a chained station about 10 m higher lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of this pitch on the descent.
A chimney climbed by stemming and scrounging; it is often wet and can feel harder than the crux late in the day. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
An easier, fun pitch up blocky ground, ending about 30 m below the summit.
A steep friction finish to the summit that looks easy from the belay but has few holds; well bolted and airy. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.

review.changed: Kept every stored label and fact; added linking and wet-pitch detail for P1-7, the two bolts at the start of P8 and the ramp downclimb, the P13 full rope length and flake cams plus the ramp length and landmarks for P13-18. Did not write a rappel table: sources only say all rappels are chained double-rope (2 x 60 m) stations taking 2.5-4 hours, with the P8 ramp downclimbed; no source lists stations, lengths or counts, and the stored 20-25 rappels note already says the count differs.
review.other_findings: Grades for the route differ by source: 5.10b in the earlier write-up, 5.10c as the crux in the later report. No Mountain Project route page was found. Stored P11 is 5.10b and P20 is labelled only 5.10 (not 5.10c).

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at a tree well to the right of the arete proper. Easy, straightforward climbing leads to a good block stance. Parties traversing in from the Caves side rarely see the tree and rope up about 40 ft above it; make an intermediate belay there, because a flake catches the rope and makes belaying the second to the next start awkward.

The most sustained and serious pitch. The line is flaring and partly off-width. An old piton sits at the crux bulge but only protects once the move is made, so back it up with a small cam (about a 0.75) and be solid. The belay is a huge ledge. It is possible to escape right from here with two rappels (a 60 m rope was used; a 50 m rope may not reach without leaving gear).

The original line crosses back and forth over the arete on a roofy pitch through a black rock band, starting just left of the arete on a runout but easy face before returning to the right side. Fun face climbing with roof pulls that finishes at a good belay ledge. A committing 5.9 variant goes right off the ledge and works back left into the black band.

Traverse left; gear is available before moving around the arete, but a second's fall on the traverse swings out and off the arete. Then climb good holds up through the black rock and traverse back right across quartz on a delicate sequence of sequential footholds. A fixed piece on the traverse is worn and worth backing up with a cam. The belay is a sloping ledge with a fixed pin and a gear seam. A sustained 5.8 variant stays right of the arete.

Climb cracks and face moves left of the sloping ledge to a horizontal knife-edge. A steeper 5.9 fingers-to-hand crack through a short quartz band sits directly in front of the belay, with jugs to help through an off-balance move and big exposure below. From the knife-edge, a short leapfrog gets you to a tree.

The standard way goes down and right roughly 150 ft into a gully and then up a weakness (about 5.5). The more direct line is a 5.8 hand and fist crack in front of the tree, with sustained fist jams and poor feet. A 5.9+ to 5.10a variant takes the arete crest more directly on the left, and a 5.9 option stays left of the arete. Belay on an easy slab.
Easy ground for a couple of hundred feet up and left, then back right. Soloing, simul-climbing or belaying all work. The walk-off appears obvious on the right.

review.changed: Wrote seven pitch notes from the route description plus photo captions of a second ascent write-up. Left out lengths, bolt counts and anchors (none stated). Pitch 6 grade shown as a range because the standard line and the hand-crack line differ. No rappel table: the route is a walk-off (SE ridge past Amphitheater Lake, or the SW couloir); the only rappels mentioned are the two for the escape after P2, which are noted in P2. Mountain Project comments could not be read (they are not in the static page).
review.other_findings: Stored overview lists the crux as pitch 4 (jam-and-lieback crack); sources put the sustained crux on pitch 2 and call pitch 4 a traverse and quartz-face pitch. Sources disagree on whether pitch numbers shift with the direct-start variations. Stored grade 5.8 is consistent; some sources quote 5.9 or 5.9+ for the harder variants.

pitch_detail.notes: The common start is the first three pitches of the neighbouring route Remorse, which keeps the overall grade at 5.9. It begins almost where the approach trail meets the wall: mid-fifth-class broken blocks to a good ledge belay.
Climb cracks straight up a short way, then trend left to a thin flake and keep traversing left below it to a ledge belay.

A chimney and blocks lead to the ledge where Outer Space proper begins. The original easier start (5.7, one or two pitches that can be simul-climbed) instead goes up a left-trending corner and scramble and then traverses past a fixed sling to the large ledge with bushes; it is easy to lose the route here.

Start up a hard crack or the dihedral to its left, reach a roof, then step out right on the famous exposed finger traverse and follow the crack right until it heads up again. Protection is good but rope drag builds. Some of the flakes on the lower crack are hollow, and one key flake was thought to have been torn off in 2021, so check holds and gear. Belay on a sloping ledge.

Move left from the belay on an easy slab with knobs, then make exposed face moves to a right-facing dihedral forming the right side of a pedestal. The dihedral is the crux of the pitch. Top out, clip the bolt above, and traverse to the left side of the pedestal to belay at the base of the splitter. It is longer than it looks and drags on the rope.

The standout pitch: a long splitter hand crack through the shield, with bomber jams and knobs on the face when the arms tire. Doubles or triples in hand sizes help avoid running out of gear. It ends on a perfect ledge with a separate crack for the anchor.

A bouldery move leaves the ledge, then the crack continues as easy jamming to the top. Gear goes up to about 3.5 inches. A 70 m rope reaches the summit boulder, which takes small gear, but not the trees 30 ft further. Save small cams or bring the second up before the low-angle chickenhead finish; the last stretch to the top is about 50 ft of scrambling.

review.changed: Used the seven-pitch layout that matches the stored count (Remorse start for pitches 1-3, Outer Space proper for 4-7). One source counts the regular start as a combined 5.7 pitch 1-2 and six pitches overall; those pitch numbers shift by one. Left out lengths because the two sources give different figures for the main crack pitch. No rappel table: the normal descent is a walk-off down gullies on climber's left; the Shield can be rappelled with double 60 m ropes in three raps to Two-Tree Ledge plus one long stretchy rap, which is an occasional alternative only and was not detailed enough for a table.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.9 and seven pitches are consistent with the Remorse-start version. Mountain Project lists 6 pitches. Comments could not be read (not in the static page).

pitch_detail.notes: Start in a corner beneath an east-facing orange panel at the toe of the buttress. Climb a blocky weakness, make a strenuous move left to a dihedral on the lowest pillar, and follow a hand crack to a belay on a nice ledge atop the pillar. This is part of the three-pitch direct start that replaces the original first two pitches (5.6 and 5.8).

The physical and mental crux. Step left around the corner from the belay into a dihedral with blocks, make a bouldery move to a rail sticking out about a foot with a flake above it, then climb left around a corner and across the face to a belay in the wide crack that splits the lower buttress. Sporty, gear-protected, with a serious feel.

Climb the steep splitter for about 35 m, step right to an obvious ledge, then follow a less strenuous corner to a pedestal at the top of the pillar with a large diving-board block. The belay takes medium nuts.

Climb through a wide section past a ledge to the steep, right-leaning crack, sustained hands to fists, passing an old homemade hanger in the wall to the right of the crack. Follow the crack to its end, trend right over blocky terrain, and belay in blocks in the middle of the buttress. Aid on the first ascent.
Climb up and left to a crack in a corner with a block above forming a keyhole. Belay under the block.
Go about 5 m left from the belay into a chimney system and make wide moves to a blocky exit onto the bivy ledge used by the first ascent party.

Several options leave the bivy ledge: a splitter crack on the left, a dihedral center-right, or a broken crack system trending right. The right option goes through a small roof to blocky terrain below the upper headwall. With a 70 m rope belay at the headwall base; with a 60 m rope belay short and scramble about 10 m of easy third class to the base.

The money pitch. Start in the perfect hand crack to the right of the off-width splitter. It widens a bit, then pinches to tight hands and ring locks before merging with the wide crack from the left. Hero moves lead to a ledge with a dodgy angle piton; a #6 cam makes a convenient belay, otherwise use small gear and chockstones.

A flaky layback leads to small footholds, then a 10 m traverse right to a good vertical hand crack. Follow it to blocky terrain and belay in a corner at large blocks. Steep and bouldery in the dihedral, with excellent movement; aided at A2 originally. A second source rates it 5.10+ while the original route description gives 5.9, so treat the grade as a range.
Climb the short steep corner and the broken face just left of it to blocky, easier terrain that tops out the Aiguille. Walk off.

review.changed: Wrote all ten pitches with metre lengths and grades as stated on the route description, which agrees with the free-ascent write-up on the crux (pitch 2), the hand-and-fist crack on pitch 4 and the dihedral on pitch 9. Pitch 9 grade given as 5.10+ while the route page lists 5.9 for it; the AAC article calls it 5.10+. No bolt counts or anchor types are stated, so none were written. No rappel table: walk-off.
review.other_findings: Stored overview says the money pitch is P8 (matches) and the bivy ledge follows P6 (matches). The stored length_m of 376 is roughly the sum of the stated pitch lengths (about 395 m) and the 1,230 ft quoted by the AAC article (375 m); consistent. Original 1978 route had a different two-pitch start (5.6 then 5.8).

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the double crack left of the giant flake. Climb right of two thin cracks until they split, follow the left fork to cruxy face moves past one bolt, then easier face climbing to a two-bolt belay. Length is estimated.

Step left to an exposed arete and climb up and right past a short system of parallel cracks, then up and right over face and chickenheads, arching left to a comfortable ledge with a small pine tree. Some parties continue about 20 ft to a belay on large chickenheads.

Continue up the face left of the large flake, past one bolt, for about 160 ft to a belay on an obvious sea of chickenheads. Slings and runners on the knobs make good gear and anchors. Length is estimated.
Climb the remaining chickenheads to a bolted move over a large flake or corner, then up and right past another bolt and over a blocky lip to a two-bolt belay on a ledge.
Extremely fun climbing over a sea of chickenheads, past two bolts, to a large toothy dike where you can belay, or continue about 30 ft of slab to a belay in an obvious seam.
A sixth short stretch of fourth-class slabbing, 100 to 200 ft, leads to the summit. Many parties count the climb as five pitches.

rappel_detail.anchor: bolts on west side of summit
rappel_detail.station: Find the rappel anchors on the west side of the summit.
rappel_detail.notes: A free-hanging rappel of about 140 ft to the saddle with two ropes, then scramble down the drainage to the base. A single 70 m rope also works if you accept about 15 ft of easy downclimbing at the bottom.
hazards: single-rope option leaves a short downclimb

review.changed: Wrote pitch notes from the route's pitch-by-pitch description. Per-pitch grades are not stated (the route is 5.8 overall), so none were written except the fourth-class finish. Stated pitch lengths are estimates in the source; converted to metres. One rappel entry from the descent text. Comments could not be read.
review.other_findings: Stored descent (double-rope rappel from a 2-bolt anchor) is consistent. Another listing gives 700 ft / six pitches (the sixth being fourth-class); a different source says the face is about 600 ft.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the crack system about 30 ft left of the descent gully. Aid up the crack, passing a false belay, to a belay about 130 ft up. Much of it could be free climbed at a moderate grade. Triples of #2 and #3 and doubles of #4 help if aiding and not back-cleaning.
Continue up the crack system into a flaring groove.
Continue up the obvious line to a ledge at the base of the Finger. Pin scars and holes off the belay make for brief but tricky aiding, and some free moves are mandatory and committing.

Traverse the ledge around the corner (about 5.6) to an ancient bolt, aid the tricky roof (about A2), and continue to a belay on the far side of the Finger. The traverse is protected by old drilled angles and a star drive; fixed tricams and fixed pins at the start of the roof are old and sketchy. A screamer helps for anchor falls. This gets you to the base of the Finger.

Scramble to a drilled pin, then climb the strenuous flare (aid C1, or free about 5.10). At its top, 5.8 grovelling is needed to reach the belay, which ends standing on the ridge with the Duck in front of you.
Traverse around the left side of the Duck. On its far side is the anchor for the descent rappels. Continue up the wide crack system to a large ledge, a bivy site, and belay.

Traverse right around the arete to a seam and aid it (about A2) back to the crest. Mixed free (5.7-5.8) and aid (C2) past questionable fixed gear leads to an exposed stance on the arete; placements and a fixed pin lead to many bolts to anchor.

Mixed free (5.7-5.8) and aid (C2, long reaches) past old fixed gear to a wide crack. Continue up it, over a roof in the caprock with wild exposure, and mantle to the belay. Nearly a bolt ladder, with free moves and top steps.
Fourth-class scrambling to the summit.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the top of pitch 7.

rappel_detail.station: Top of pitch 7, on the arete.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the anchor beside the Duck at the top of pitch 6.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three double-rope rappels down the descent gully to the base.
Second double-rope rappel in the gully.
Third double-rope rappel to the base. A shortcut of two double-rope rappels to the west down the cliff near the base saves walking around the tower.

review.changed: Wrote nine pitch entries with aid grades and feet converted to metres; the ninth is the fourth-class summit scramble. Rappels follow the descent text (P8 to P7, P7 to the Duck, three double-rope raps down the gully); the source gives no anchor types or lengths, so none were written. Comments could not be read.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches=8 and 5.8 C2+; the source lists 9 including the fourth-class summit. Another reference gives 9 pitches and A2+.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble the fourth-class approach ramp (rope up if you might fall) to a large flat area, then start at a short fingertip crack. It is low and quick, with one good fingerlock to lunge for. Two ways reach the first ramp belay: a short right-facing dihedral then a traverse right, or a traverse right to the same ramp.

Reach the right-facing Ruper crack by traversing or downclimbing right about 30 ft. It is a roughly 5-inch crack at the back of a flaring dihedral; ripples for lips and feet keep it at 5.8. Bring a #3.5 or #4 cam, and use side cracks higher up. The Rover variation on the left side of the block is easier than it looks but still about 5.9.

Begins with a wildly airy thin friction traverse over a slight bulge, then a fun dihedral to a big belay ledge, the Upper Ramp. Doubles help protect the follower on the traverse: clip only one rope while leading the dihedral so the other acts as a top rope. Rappelling off is possible after these first three pitches.

After a short fourth-class scramble, climb a short protectable dihedral, then work left onto runout 5.6 face climbing on solid, juggy rock. A fall in the wrong spot lands on the belay ledge. Belay on a tiny shelf.
A short pitch to a cramped pod under a huge roof. The anchor is two old pins backed up with a marginal cam between fractured blocks.

Traverse under the roof past three old pitons, with good cam and nut placements that should be used instead. A few reachy 5.8 moves past a hidden jug end the technical climbing, then about 40 ft of easy runout ground leads to a belay tree. The 5.8 move is poorly protected by two unreliable pins; the upper section is runout 5.5 and wet after rain or snow. A 15-minute scramble leads to the summit of Tower One.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches combining the route's own description (two three-pitch halves split at the Upper Ramp, the crack and the Rover variation, the last pitch's weak protection) with a detailed ascent account of each pitch. The two sources do not agree on the exact grade of each pitch, so only grades stated by a source were used. No lengths, bolt counts or rappel table (descent is a scramble off the summit; rappelling off after pitch 3 is mentioned only in P3).
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.8+ matches the start; another source says 5.8. Comments could not be read.
